newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Patriarch urges caution on Lenin removal.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Patriarch urges caution on Lenin removal.

text.p: Russian Orthodox Patriarch Alexiy II on Thursday urged extra caution in deciding whether to remove the mummified body of the founder of the Soviet state, Vladimir Lenin, from his Red Square mausoleum in Moscow.

"Of course it's for the people to decide," Alexiy told reporters, referring to President Boris Yeltsin's proposal to ask Russians about the fate of Lenin's body, which has lain in state since his death in 1924.
"But my personal opinion is that one should not undertake steps which could further split troubled Russian society," the patriarch added.

Yeltsin has long campaigned for Lenin's removal, saying it was un-Christian to keep a dead body on display and arguing that the communist leader, who he says put Russia on a wrong track for more than 70 years, himself wanted to be buried.

The Kremlin leader renewed his crusade earlier this month by proposing to ask Russians in a referendum whether they want Lenin and dozens of other leading Soviet figures buried next to the mausoleum to be taken away.
Yeltsin has said that the referendum could take place in the autumn, prompting angry reaction from the Communist opposition.
The communists have aggressively denounced plans to re-bury Lenin, saying that noone can deny his role in turning the Soviet Union into a superpower feared by the rest of the world.
They also say that Lenin did not express any wish for the fate of his body and point to many Orthodox saints whose mummies are carefully preserved by the Church.
The communists warn that an attempt to remove Lenin from the Red Square could prompt public unrest around the country.

But Yeltsin's camp insists that relative political stability and the time which has passed since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 have made the fate of Lenin's body an academic issue unlikely to inflame public opinion in the country.
The latest opinion polls show that Russians are split roughly 50/50 over Lenin's re-burial.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union Yeltsin removed guards of honour from the mausoleum but it is still open to the public.
Yeltsin's aides have said that the Kremlin leader was still examining public reaction to his proposals and that he so far has no plan of what to do with the body and the mausoleum.
Maverick ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky offered earlier this week to buy the mummy and take it on a money-making roadshow around the world.
